sections.title: What You'll Learn
sections.content:
Ever wondered why 2 + 3 * 4 equals 14 and not 20? Let's crack the code of how Java evaluates expressions!

• How Java decides the order of operations
• Why parentheses are your best friends
• How to avoid common calculation mistakes

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
Imagine you're at a restaurant with a special order rule: drinks first, then appetizers, then main course. Java follows similar rules when evaluating expressions!

Java uses **operator precedence** - a set of rules that determines which operations happen first. Here's how it works:

• **Parentheses** always win - they're like putting something in a VIP section
• **Multiplication/Division** come next - they're the appetizers
• **Addition/Subtraction** come last - they're the main course

For example: `3 + 4 * 2` equals 11, not 14, because multiplication happens before addition.

sections.title: Code Examples
Key Points
points: Multiplication, division, and modulus have higher precedence than addition and subtraction
Parentheses override the default precedence and are evaluated first
Operators of equal precedence are evaluated left to right (left-associative)
The assignment operator = is right-associative: a = b = 5 assigns 5 to both b and a
Always use parentheses when the evaluation order is ambiguous

sections.title: Summary
sections.content: Operator precedence determines the order of operations in Java. Parentheses > Multiplication/Division > Addition/Subtraction. Practice breaking down complex expressions step by step.

questions.question: What is the result of: 2 + 3 * 4 - 1?
questions.explanation: Following operator precedence: multiplication first (3 * 4 = 12), then left to right for addition and subtraction (2 + 12 - 1 = 13).

questions.question: How can you override the default operator precedence in Java?
questions.explanation: Parentheses () are used to override default operator precedence. Expressions inside parentheses are evaluated first. For example, (2 + 3) * 4 = 20.
